## Citizen Science: The Role of Volunteers in the Census

The transformation of the Charca de Suárez cannot be explained solely by public investment or by the administrative files advancing through the offices of the Junta de Andalucía. There is a less visible but equally decisive component that operates every month with the regularity of clockwork: the network of volunteers who, since 2010, dedicate their mornings to counting birds, checking nests, and recording species with the patience of those who understand that conservation is built on concrete data. Coordinated by the Spanish Ornithological Society, SEO/BirdLife, these citizens have turned amateur observation into a first-rate scientific tool.

The Charca's citizen science program operates with a rigorous methodology that has little to envy professional censuses. Each month, volunteers walk the wetland's trails with binoculars and field notebooks, recording the number of individuals of each species, their spatial distribution, and the reproductive behaviors they detect. Nest monitoring occupies a central part of the work, especially during spring, when pairs of waterbirds settle in the reed beds and the artificial islets created to encourage breeding. The data collected does not remain in local archives: it feeds national and international databases, including the waterbird monitoring program coordinated by Wetlands International, one of the most extensive monitoring networks on the planet.

The program's continuity over more than a decade has made it possible to build long time series, a statistical treasure rarely available to natural areas managed with limited resources. Those series are what reveal population trends that would otherwise go unnoticed: the silent decline of a migratory species, the progressive increase of another that finds an increasingly stable refuge in the Charca, or the sporadic appearance of rare birds that volunteers document with photographs and detailed descriptions. Each observation recorded in a field notebook becomes, over time, a point on a curve that technicians can interpret to make management decisions.

Scientific bird ringing is another pillar of the program. Volunteers participate in periodic sessions of capture, marking, and release of birds, a technique that provides individualized information on migratory routes, longevity, and site fidelity. A bird ringed at the Charca de Suárez may be recaptured months later in a wetland in northern Europe; that seemingly anecdotal piece of data contributes to mapping the ecological connectivity that underpins conservation policies on a continental scale. Collaboration with SEO/BirdLife ensures that capture and handling protocols meet the ethical and technical standards required by European regulations.

Early detection of threats is perhaps the most tangible benefit of this citizen network. Volunteers who visit the Charca regularly develop a familiarity with the ecosystem that allows them to notice subtle changes: a drop in water levels, the proliferation of an invasive species, the presence of discharges, or the alteration of marsh vegetation. This informal but systematic surveillance has alerted municipal authorities and site managers on several occasions, triggering rapid responses that would likely have arrived too late if they depended exclusively on periodic inspections. Citizen science functions, in this sense, as a low-cost, highly effective early warning system.

The profile of volunteers is diverse and reflects the Charca's ability to mobilize the local community. Retirees who discovered in ornithology a late passion, biology students seeking field experience, teachers who incorporate the censuses into their educational projects, and Motril residents who simply want to better know the natural area just minutes from home. This heterogeneity enriches the program, because each participant brings a different perspective and a level of commitment adapted to their possibilities. The ongoing training offered by SEO/BirdLife levels knowledge and ensures data quality, regardless of each observer's prior experience.

The program's educational dimension is inseparable from its scientific value. Volunteers do not only collect data: they learn to identify species, interpret behaviors, and understand the complex interactions that sustain the wetland ecosystem. That knowledge then spreads through their family and social circles, generating a culture of appreciation for biodiversity that transcends the boundaries of the Charca. The monthly censuses thus become a permanent school of amateur naturalists, whose effects multiply throughout the Motril community.

Collaboration between local administration and the associative fabric has been fundamental to sustaining the program over the years. The Motril City Council facilitates access to the site, provides logistical support for ringing sessions, and publicly recognizes the volunteers' work, while SEO/BirdLife contributes technical coordination, training, and connection to national and international monitoring networks. This alliance between the public and the citizen explains, to a large extent, why the Charca de Suárez today has an ornithological database that many wetlands of greater size and budget would envy.

The results accumulated since 2010 have served to support specific management decisions. Information on the species that use the Charca as a wintering area or migratory stopover has justified investments in habitat improvement, regulation of water levels, and creation of new refuge areas. Volunteer data has also been incorporated into the reports supporting the application for designation as a Special Protection Area for Birds, the European recognition that will definitively consolidate the site's protection. Citizen science, far from being a decorative complement, has become a pillar of wetland management.

The program's future lies in expanding the base of participants and diversifying tasks. The monthly waterbird censuses could be complemented with monitoring of amphibians, dragonflies, or vegetation, broadening the scope of biological monitoring. The incorporation of new technologies, such as mobile apps for recording observations or digital citizen science platforms, would facilitate participation by people with less time availability. The Charca de Suárez demonstrates that biodiversity conservation is not exclusively a matter for scientists and administrations: the citizens who approach the wetland with curiosity and persistence are, in many ways, the best guardians of its future.
